title: Pascha
hookLine: Christ is risen! Truly he is risen!

cards: Near midnight, and the church is dark. Not dim. Dark.
Everyone is holding an unlit candle.

Then the priest comes out from behind the icon screen holding a single flame, and the light starts to travel, his candle to the first person's, theirs to the next, until the whole room is gold and flickering.

The people follow him outside and walk around the church in the night air, singing. At the closed front doors, the priest calls out a short greeting, and the crowd shouts back an answer, loud enough to wake the street.

teach.h: CHRIST OUR PASCH: THE NEW PASSOVER.
teach.b: Pascha is what Eastern Christians call Easter. Paul ties it straight to the Passover lamb: in the Douay-Rheims, "For Christ our pasch is sacrificed." The pasch is the Passover.
Easter, for these churches, is the new Passover, the night God leads his people from death into life. Then the greeting. Christ is risen!
Truly he is risen! It's said in Greek, Arabic, Ukrainian, Malayalam, Ge'ez, the languages of the churches we've visited. The answer isn't decoration.
It echoes the first Easter evening in Luke, when the disciples tell each other, "The Lord is risen indeed." Indeed. Truly.

teach.h: TRULY HE IS RISEN: A WITNESS SAID BACK.
teach.b: It's a witness, said back. And people keep saying it, as a hello and a goodbye, through the Easter season.
Then the hymn they sing outside the doors, which the Byzantine churches repeat over and over: Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death, and giving life to those in the tombs.

teach.h: THE TABLE IS SET FOR ALL.
teach.b: Last, a sermon read aloud at the midnight liturgy, attributed to Saint John Chrysostom.
It invites everyone to the feast: those who fasted the whole of Lent, those who came at the last hour, and those who didn't fast at all. Nobody should go away hungry, it says.
Nobody should mourn their failings, because forgiveness has risen from the tomb. After a strict Lent, that's not the moment to check who kept the rules. The table is set for all.

how: Eastern Catholics celebrate Pascha at a night service with candles, a procession around the church and the repeated greeting "Christ is risen! Truly he is risen!", and use the greeting in place of hello throughout the Easter season.

o: the Eastern name for the Last Supper
the Eastern churches' name for Easter

s: the answer "truly he is risen" echoes Luke's Gospel
on the first Easter evening the disciples say "the Lord is risen indeed."
the Paschal sermon read at midnight scolds those who didn't fast
it invites everyone to the feast, even those who came at the last hour.
Pascha is linked to the Passover
Paul writes "Christ our pasch is sacrificed": the pasch is the Passover lamb.

games.q: it's Easter week. an Eastern Catholic friend greets you: "Christ is risen!" what's the traditional reply?
games.why: "truly he is risen!" the answer is a witness said back, echoing the disciples in Luke: the Lord is risen indeed.

practice: Say the greeting quietly a few times, Christ is risen, truly he is risen, letting the second line come a little stronger, the way a crowd answers.
Picture someone you could greet this way at Easter, a friend, a grandparent, someone in a parish hall, and their face as they answer.
If you pray, the greeting itself can be your prayer; if you don't, hold it as a sentence shouted at midnight in many languages, and notice how it lands.

wordCard.voice: Pascha. The Eastern name for Easter, the new Passover, the feast of Christ's resurrection, opened at midnight with candles and a shouted greeting. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: Christ is risen, the Easter greeting; the reply is Ἀληθῶς ἀνέστη, truly he is risen.

carryVoice: Your line: truly he is risen. It's a witness, said back a little stronger. See you tomorrow.
